title: Tensor Shapes & Ranks Deep Dive 📐
description: Go beyond the basics: rank, shape, size, and how to inspect tensors thoroughly.

slides.title: Rank, Shape, Size Recap 🧠
slides.content:
# Tensor Anatomy
- **Rank** = number of dimensions (axes).
- **Shape** = length along each axis.
- **Size** = total number of elements (product of shape).

Example: `tf.constant([[1,2,3],[4,5,6]])`
- Rank: 2
- Shape: `(2, 3)`
- Size: 6

> Analogy: Think of a spreadsheet – rows × columns.

slides.title: Inspecting Tensors 🔍
slides.codeSnippet:
import tensorflow as tf

t = tf.constant([[[1,2],[3,4]],[[5,6],[7,8]]])
print('Rank:', tf.rank(t).numpy())       # 3
print('Shape:', t.shape)                 # (2, 2, 2)
print('Number of dims:', t.ndim)         # 3
print('Total elements:', tf.size(t).numpy())  # 8

quizData.question: What is the rank of a tensor with shape (4, 3, 2, 1)?
quizData.explanation: Rank = number of dimensions = length of the shape tuple, which is 4 here.

slides.title: Dynamic Shapes & Static Shapes 🔄
slides.content:
# Two Shape Concepts
- **Static shape**: known at graph construction time (can be partially `None`).
- **Dynamic shape**: determined at runtime.

```python
t = tf.placeholder(tf.float32, shape=[None, 3])
# Static shape: (None, 3) – first dim unknown
# Dynamic shape: (batch_size, 3) after feeding
```

In eager mode, they are usually the same, but `tf.function` graphs may differ.

slides.title: Exploring `tf.shape` vs `.shape`
slides.content: `t.shape` returns a `TensorShape` object. `tf.shape(t)` returns a tensor.
slides.codeSnippet:
t = tf.constant([[1,2],[3,4]])
print(type(t.shape))     # tensorflow.python.framework.tensor_shape.TensorShape
print(tf.shape(t))        # tf.Tensor([2 2], shape=(2,), dtype=int32)
print(tf.shape(t).numpy()) # array([2, 2])

quizData.question: True or False: In eager mode, `t.shape` always returns a tuple of integers with no `None` entries.
quizData.explanation: Even in eager mode, a tensor may have a partially defined shape if it was created with unknown dimensions (e.g., via `tf.placeholder`-like behavior in tf.function). So `None` can appear.

slides.title: Golden Rule ✨
slides.content: When debugging, **always** print `t.shape` and `t.dtype` first. 90% of errors come from mismatched shapes or types.
